turns.doctor_question: Hello, I’m Dr. ____. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Doctor. Yeah, so... I guess I'm here because things at work are just getting really frustrating. I manage a team of sales reps—non-retail, mostly corporate accounts—and I've just been making these really dumb mistakes on our sales reports. It's driving me completely crazy. 

Like, I have to pull the weekly metrics from our team dashboard, right? And I'll just end up copying the wrong numbers entirely. I'll put the wrong figure in the wrong box, or I'll be going through one of the standard operating procedures I'm supposed to check off on for the team, and I'll just completely miss a line. Just skip right over it. And the worst part is, I really thought I went over it! I'll sit there, stare at the monitor, double-check it, and think it's perfect. Then an hour later my manager is emailing me asking why the totals don't match up or why a compliance check was left blank. 

It's embarrassing, honestly. I'm 36, I'm the supervisor, I'm supposed to be the one catching their errors, not the one messing up basic data entry. I've tried using a ruler on the screen, printing it out, whatever, but it just keeps happening and it's making me look really incompetent to the higher-ups. It's just... I don't know, it feels like no matter how hard I try to focus on those little details, my brain just edits them out, and I'm worried it's going to cost me my job if I don't figure out why I keep doing this.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient explicitly describes making careless mistakes on sales reports, such as copying wrong numbers and missing lines in procedures despite double-checking, which indicates a failure to give close attention to details.

turns.doctor_question: Did you have similar trouble with inattention or careless mistakes when you were a child, before age 12?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, honestly... I was exactly like this as a kid, too. It’s funny you ask that, because my mom actually still brings it up. She kept all these old report cards and notes from my teachers in elementary school—like second grade, third grade, all the way up. I remember Mrs. Gable in third grade, she would write these long notes home complaining about me. 

The notes always said the exact same things. They’d say I rushed through my work, which was true, I would just blaze through my math worksheets in like five minutes just so I could be done, and I'd get half of it wrong just from careless mistakes, not because I didn't know how to do the math. And the homework... man, my backpack was like a total black hole. My mom would go in there and find crumpled up assignments from three weeks ago stuffed at the bottom under a bunch of wrappers and old gym clothes. I lost everything. 

And it wasn't just the schoolwork, either. The teachers were always writing that I talked out of turn, just blurting things out in the middle of a lesson because a thought popped into my head and I just felt like I had to say it right that second. And sitting still? Forget it. They had to constantly remind me to stay in my seat. I was always getting up to sharpen my pencil, or throw something away, or I'd just be leaning over bothering the kid next to me. It's like, even back then, I just couldn't do the quiet, careful thing they wanted me to do. So yeah, it's definitely not a new thing at all, it's just... I don't know, the stakes are just so much higher now, you know? Back then it was just a bad grade or a note home, but now it's my actual livelihood and my corporate accounts on the line, so I really need to get a handle on it.

symptom_reasoning.S001: The patient confirms making careless mistakes on math worksheets as a child.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient describes their childhood backpack as a 'black hole' with crumpled assignments stuffed at the bottom, indicating severe disorganization.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient explicitly states they 'lost everything' regarding schoolwork and assignments.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient notes they could not stay seated in class and were always getting up to sharpen pencils or throw things away.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient recalls blurting things out in the middle of lessons when a thought popped into their head.
